At 6:12 every morning, the town’s old clock tower rang thirteen times.

No one knew why. The clock had been repaired, inspected, and politely threatened. The gears were clean. The bell was intact. Still: thirteen.

People built their mornings around it. Bakers slid loaves into the oven on the twelfth chime. Children raced for the school bus on the thirteenth. The mayor called it a charming tradition, though he had never once arrived at work before seven.

Then, one Tuesday in November, the tower rang twelve times.

The town stopped.

A woman on Main Street lowered her coffee. A dog dropped a stick. In the bakery, a tray of rolls burned while the baker stood listening to the silence where the final note should have been.

By noon, people had begun asking what it meant.

By supper, they had decided it meant something terrible.

The mayor gathered everyone in the town hall and announced a committee. The committee announced a subcommittee. The subcommittee concluded that the missing chime was probably a mechanical issue, but recommended forming a task force to investigate the possibility of a message.

At 6:12 the next morning, the clock rang thirteen times.

Everyone sighed with relief.

Except for a little girl named June, who had been awake all night. She sat on the front steps of the library, wrapped in her grandfather’s coat, and listened to the last chime fade over the rooftops.

Her grandfather had died that spring. He used to say the clock wasn’t keeping time. It was keeping company.

June thought about this, then stood and walked to the tower. The door was unlocked. Inside, the air smelled like dust and cold iron. She climbed the narrow stairs until the town lay beneath her in a patchwork of chimneys and streetlamps.

She found the clock mechanism turning steadily, its brass heart beating without fuss.

Nothing was wrong.

When she got down, she told no one what she’d seen. Some things are easier to hear when you aren’t explaining them.

The next morning, at 6:12, the clock rang thirteen times. People began their days.

And somewhere, inside the old tower, one small gear turned on—faithful, mysterious, keeping company with the dark.
